cards.front: Which immunoglobulin class is naturally occurring anti-A and anti-B (isohemagglutinins)?
cards.back: Predominantly IgM (with some IgG component); they react best at room temperature / immediate spin.

cards.front: Anti-[[1]] (isohemagglutinins) react best at room temperature; immune anti-[[2]] reacts best at the AHG phase.
cards.back: 1: A/B  2: D (Rh)

cards.front: What is the rule for handling weak D in donors versus recipients?
cards.back: Weak D donor units are issued as Rh-positive; weak D patients are treated as Rh-negative and receive Rh-negative red cells.
cards.note: Classic exam pair — the rule flips by role.

cards.front: Group O red cells have [[1]] A/B antigens and group O plasma contains [[2]].
cards.back: 1: no (neither)  2: anti-A and anti-B (both)
cards.note: O has nO antigens and bOth antibodies.

cards.front: Which sugar does the A transferase add to H substance to create the A antigen?
cards.back: N-acetylgalactosamine (the B transferase adds galactose; the common O allele makes a nonfunctional transferase).

cards.front: Why is reverse (serum) typing unreliable in newborns?
cards.back: Naturally occurring anti-A and anti-B are not yet reliably produced; isohemagglutinins mature over the first months of life. Forward typing (antigens) works at birth.

cards.front: Forward typing tests [[1]] on patient red cells; reverse typing tests [[2]] in patient plasma.
cards.back: 1: A/B antigens  2: anti-A/anti-B antibodies

cards.front: What is acquired B, and in what clinical settings does it classically occur?
cards.back: Bacterial enzymes (deacetylases) modify A antigen so group A cells react with anti-B reagent; classically in gram-negative sepsis or colorectal disease. The patient's plasma still contains anti-B.
cards.note: Forward looks AB, reverse proves group A.

cards.front: Which lectin distinguishes A1 cells from weaker A subgroups such as A2?
cards.back: Dolichos biflorus lectin (agglutinates A1 strongly; weak/nonreactive with A2 and weaker subgroups).

cards.front: Rouleaux in reverse typing is resolved with the [[1]] technique; true agglutination [[2]] after the wash.
cards.back: 1: saline replacement  2: persists (remains)

cards.front: Which red cell antigen is the most immunogenic after ABO?
cards.back: The D antigen of the Rh system; anti-D is IgG, AHG-reactive, crosses the placenta.

cards.front: The direct antiglobulin test (DAT) detects [[1]] bound to patient red cells [[2]].
cards.back: 1: IgG and/or complement  2: in vivo (in the patient)

cards.front: How does RhIg prevent Rh sensitization?
cards.back: Passive anti-D clears fetal D-positive red cells from the maternal circulation before her immune system can mount an active response.

cards.front: Compare Rh HDFN and ABO HDFN: parity and severity.
cards.back: Rh HDFN: usually second/later pregnancies, can be severe, DAT strongly positive. ABO HDFN: often firstborn, usually mild, DAT often weak or negative.

cards.front: In Rh HDFN, maternal [[1]] anti-D crosses the placenta and binds [[2]] fetal red cells.
cards.back: 1: IgG  2: D-positive

cards.front: What is the difference between weak D and partial D?
cards.back: Weak D: reduced number of D antigen sites (usually not immunogenic). Partial D: altered/missing D epitopes — the patient can form anti-D against the missing epitopes.

cards.front: Which monospecific DAT pattern is typical of warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia vs cold agglutinin disease?
cards.back: Warm AIHA: DAT positive with anti-IgG. Cold agglutinin disease: DAT positive mainly with anti-C3 (complement).

cards.front: A positive DAT proves red cell sensitization [[1]]; it does not by itself prove [[2]].
cards.back: 1: in vivo  2: hemolysis (active destruction)

cards.front: Name the classic indications for performing a DAT on a patient.
cards.back: Suspected HDFN, suspected hemolytic transfusion reaction, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, and drug-induced immune hemolysis.

cards.front: Why can RhIg administration complicate serologic interpretation after delivery?
cards.back: Passive anti-D can appear in the maternal antibody screen and weakly coat the baby's D-positive cells (weak DAT); distinguish passive from active sensitization by timing and titer trends.

title: Transfusion Practice: Panels, Crossmatch, Reactions, Components

cards.front: Why are reagent red cells for antibody screens chosen to be homozygous for common antigens?
cards.back: Dosage: homozygous cells give stronger reactions, making true negatives clearer and rule-outs more reliable.

cards.front: In antibody identification, an antibody is ruled out when its antigen is present on a cell that did [[1]]; the pattern of [[2]] cells confirms the specificity.
cards.back: 1: not react  2: reacting

cards.front: What does the immediate-spin phase of the crossmatch detect?
cards.back: ABO incompatibility (IgM isohemagglutinins) between donor red cells and recipient plasma.

cards.front: When is an electronic (computer) crossmatch acceptable?
cards.back: When the antibody screen is negative and there is no history of unexpected antibodies, under a validated quality system per local policy.

cards.front: Acute hemolytic transfusion reactions are most often caused by [[1]] incompatibility, usually from [[2]] error.
cards.back: 1: ABO  2: clerical (identification/labeling)

cards.front: List the immediate laboratory workup of a suspected acute hemolytic transfusion reaction.
cards.back: Stop transfusion; clerical check of records/labels; DAT on post-reaction sample; visual inspection of plasma/urine; repeat ABO typing of patient and unit; hemolysis markers.

cards.front: How does TRALI differ from TACO?
cards.back: TRALI: noncardiogenic lung injury within 6 hours, bilateral infiltrates, hypoxemia, no overload. TACO: volume overload with hypertension, dyspnea, pulmonary edema, treated with diuresis.

cards.front: Febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reactions are a diagnosis of [[1]] after excluding [[2]] and bacterial contamination.
cards.back: 1: exclusion  2: hemolysis

cards.front: Which component is richest in fibrinogen and is used for hypofibrinogenemia?
cards.back: Cryoprecipitate (also contains factor VIII, von Willebrand factor, and factor XIII).

cards.front: Match the modification to its purpose: leukoreduction, irradiation, washing.
cards.back: Leukoreduction: fewer febrile reactions, less HLA alloimmunization, lower CMV risk. Irradiation: prevents TA-GVHD. Washing: removes plasma (e.g., IgA-deficient patients with anti-IgA).

cards.front: Delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions occur [[1]] after transfusion from an [[2]] antibody response (e.g., Kidd, Rh).
cards.back: 1: days to weeks  2: anamnestic (memory)

cards.front: What is the classic presentation of an anaphylactic transfusion reaction, and what deficiency is suspected?
cards.back: Severe hypotension, bronchospasm, angioedema within minutes; suspect IgA deficiency with anti-IgA in the recipient. Use washed components / IgA-deficient donor products.

cards.front: What is the primary indication for packed red cell transfusion?
cards.back: Restoring oxygen-carrying capacity in symptomatic anemia or active bleeding; triggers are clinical and restrictive strategies are evidence supported.

cards.front: Platelet transfusion treats [[1]] bleeding or prophylaxis in thrombocytopenia; refractoriness may be [[2]] (HLA/HPA antibodies) or nonimmune.
cards.back: 1: thrombocytopenic  2: immune

cards.front: Fresh frozen plasma is indicated for which clinical situations?
cards.back: Multiple coagulation factor deficiency with bleeding or before invasive procedures; it must be ABO compatible and is not a volume expander.

cards.front: What does a positive antibody screen mandate before compatible blood is issued?
cards.back: Full antibody identification, patient antigen typing, selection of antigen-negative units, and serologic (AHG) crossmatch; record the antibody permanently.

cards.front: Bacterial contamination is classically associated with [[1]] components stored at [[2]] temperature.
cards.back: 1: platelet  2: room
cards.note: Also: Yersinia can grow in refrigerated red cells.

cards.front: What is the significance of finding anti-Jka in a patient's antibody workup?
cards.back: Anti-Jka is clinically significant (can cause delayed hemolytic reactions and HDFN); the patient must receive Jka-negative blood for all future transfusions and the antibody is recorded permanently.

cards.front: Why must a pretransfusion specimen be labeled at the bedside?
cards.back: Mislabeling is a leading root cause of ABO-incompatible transfusion; bedside positive patient identification prevents wrong-blood-in-tube errors.

cards.front: The minimum required database for a patient with a known antibody includes ABO/Rh type, the antibody [[1]], and patient antigen [[2]].
cards.back: 1: specificity (identified)  2: typing (or genotyping)
